Cultural hitchhiking: burial rites and genomic variation in space and time Abstract

Cultural hitchhiking: burial rites and genomic variation in space and time Elisabetta Canteri 2025-09-08 Abstract Describing and interpreting cultural history and transmission has been a central focus of archaeology for over a century. New information coming from ancient DNA has revealed the fundamental role of demography in shaping both genomic and cultural change. Yet, the effects of demographic processes on the spatial and temporal distributions of cultural and genomic patterns are still poorly understood. Here, we examine the relations between demography and space-time patterns of genomic variation and cultural traditions, by testing whether shifts in genomic patterns correspond to spatiotemporal changes in burial rites. Our approach uses data accessed from the Big Interdisciplinary Archaeological Database (BIAD), linking mortuary information from approximately 4,200 individuals with genetic ancestry and mobility data inferred from over 1,300 human genomes, spanning vast parts of Western Eurasia over the last 10,000 years. By integrating and modeling these diverse datasets, we aim to provide a comprehensive understanding of how human mobility and demographic change intersect with cultural traditions, offering new insights into the dynamics behind culture history, and the extent to which genes and culture are transmitted in parallel.

Chapter 1 Burial data Here we are going to track the analysis on the data that Robert and Stephen shared with us. We want to explore whether we can find a relationship between large scale human migrations and changes in burial practices during he Holocene. We will analyse burial practices data against a Gaussian spatial process and values of human ancestry and mobility. The data we have are records of different burial types at grave sites across Europe. Let’s first input the data. This means that there are more than 2 descriptors for each variable. This makes it tricky because we cannot model factors with more that 2 levels. Therefore, we will create new columns in the database where we transform the factors to a binomial presence/absence data (0/1). Also, for the Burial Side variable, we have a level called “left?” in the original data table, what should we do with this? Can we group this with the left or not? For now I grouped it because it consists of just 5 records, but we can decide later whether we should keep it separate or not. Let’s plot the data to see what we are working with. 1.2 Histograms The burial orientation seems interesting because the majority of the data lies on specific angles, for example: 0, 45, 90, 135, 180, 225, and 270. The body positioning also seems to aggregate towards “crouched”, “inside a vessel”, “extended”, and “scattered”, with the two most represented groups being “crouched” and “inside a vessel”. An UpSet plot is a simplified visualization of a Venn diagram. upset_df <- graves[, .(IndividualID, BodyPositioning_crouched, BodyPositioning_extended, `BodyPositioning_extended, rhomboid`, BodyPositioning_heap, `BodyPositioning_inside a vessel`, BodyPositioning_irregular, BodyPositioning_prone, BodyPositioning_scattered, BodyPositioning_sitting, BurialSide_back, `BurialSide_back/left`, `BurialSide_back/right`, BurialSide_bottom, BurialSide_front, `BurialSide_front/left`, `BurialSide_front/right`, BurialSide_left, `BurialSide_left/back`, `BurialSide_left/front`, BurialSide_right, `BurialSide_right/back`, `BurialSide_right/front`)] # UpSet plot with all variables upset(upset_df, sets = colnames(upset_df)[-1], order.by = 'freq', keep.order = F) set_size <- data.frame(Set = colnames(upset_df)[-1], Size = colSums(upset_df[,-1], na.rm = T)) ggplot(data = set_size) + geom_bar(aes(x = reorder(Set, Size, decreasing = T), y = Size), stat = "identity") + theme_bw() + ylab("Set Size") + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1), axis.title.x = element_blank(), plot.margin = margin(t = 5, r = 10, l = 30, b = 5)) # UpSet plot with selected variables sets <- c("BodyPositioning_crouched", "BodyPositioning_extended", "BodyPositioning_heap", "BodyPositioning_inside a vessel", "BodyPositioning_prone", "BodyPositioning_scattered", "BodyPositioning_sitting","BurialSide_bottom", "BurialSide_front", "BurialSide_left", "BurialSide_right", "BurialSide_back") upset(upset_df, sets = sets, order.by = 'freq', keep.order = T, set_size.show = T) set_size <- set_size[which(set_size$Set %in% sets),] ggplot(data = set_size) + geom_bar(aes(x = reorder(Set, Size, decreasing = T), y = Size), stat = "identity") + theme_bw() + ylab("Set Size") + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1), axis.title.x = element_blank(), plot.margin = margin(t = 5, r = 10, l = 20, b = 5)) Now let’s plot the MCA biplots without the repel option. This is because both left and right are associated with the crouched position and the back is associated with the extended position, which are the most commonly found positions in graves. 2.5.1 Model fit Here we take a look at the model fit. We tested different models, with different combinations of covariates. Her we take a look at the model fit, based on WAIC and DIC scores. Because of colinearity between WHG and the other ancestries, we should exclude the full ancestry models from the evaluation of model fit. We also look at model fit for the models before 5k BP. We have the min and max, but we will work with the mean. There are cases where the min angle is the only angle available. In that case, the min will be used as the mean. We have two ways to get the mean angles: Use a custom function that we create Use the mean.circular function of the circular package. We can compare the two to see how they perform. ## We can't just average between the min and max angles because for some angles the average will be 0, so we will not get burials facing south. ## We create a function to transform the angles that works around this issue. #---------------------------------------------------------------------- find.mid.deg <- function(min.deg, max.deg){ difference <- max.deg - min.deg i.accute <- difference<180 i.obtuse <- difference>180 i.bad <- difference==180 mid <- numeric() mid[i.accute] <- max.deg[i.accute] - difference[i.accute]/2 mid[i.obtuse] <- max.deg[i.obtuse] + (360 - difference[i.obtuse])/2 mid[i.bad] <- NA i <- mid>=360 mid[i] <- mid[i]-360 i <- mid<0 mid[i] <- mid[i]+360 return(mid)} #---------------------------------------------------------------------- min.deg <- c(5,15,170,270) max.deg <- c(356,300,185,360) find.mid.deg(min.deg, max.deg) ## [1] 0.5 337.5 177.5 315.0 #---------------------------------------------------------------------- # Remove NAs in both min and max orientation columns orientation <- orientation[!(is.na(BurialOrientationMin) & is.na(BurialOrientationMax))] # Create a table for records that have a single angle value (in BurialOrientationMin) single_angles <- orientation[is.na(BurialOrientationMax)] single_angles[, BurialOrientationMean := BurialOrientationMin] # Remove from overall table orientation <- orientation[!(is.na(BurialOrientationMin) | is.na(BurialOrientationMax))] # Average across min and max ## Using Adrian's function orientation[, BurialOrientationMean := find.mid.deg(BurialOrientationMin, BurialOrientationMax)] ## Using circular package means <- round(sapply(1:nrow(orientation), function(x) mean.circular(circular(c(orientation$BurialOrientationMin[x], orientation$BurialOrientationMax[x]), type = "angles", units = "degrees", rotation = "clock"))),2) means <- sapply(1:length(means), function(x) ifelse(means[x] < 0, 360 + means[x], means[x])) ## Check differences orientation$BurialOrientationMin[698]; orientation$BurialOrientationMax[698] ## [1] 270 ## [1] 0 orientation$BurialOrientationMean[698]; means[698] ## [1] 135 ## [1] 315 In this last example we can see that the custom function we have does not recognize 270 as the minimum angle, but it takes 0 as the minimum making the mean 135. 1)){ ix <- which(between(v, bins[b], bins[b+1])) cat[ix] <- b } ix2 <- which(v %in% center.zero) cat[ix2] <- 0 return(cat) } #### -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Now that we have the function, we can create circular histograms with binwidth of 22.5, which is 360/16. 3.2 Exploration and visualization 3.2.1 All individuals ##### All individuals ###### dim_angles <- orientation[, .N, by = c("BurialOrientationMean_sin", "BurialOrientationMean_cos")] ggplot(data = dim_angles) + geom_point(aes(BurialOrientationMean_sin, BurialOrientationMean_cos, size = N), shape = 21) + scale_size_continuous("Count", breaks = c(1, 10, 50, 100, 150, 200, 250), range = c(3,10)) + xlab(expression(sin(theta))) + ylab(expression(cos(theta))) + coord_equal() + theme_bw() + theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.text = element_text(size = 14), axis.title = element_text(size = 16), legend.text = element_text(size = 14), legend.title = element_text(size = 16)) # Circular histogram w <- 22.5 orientation[, Bins := circular.bins(BurialOrientationMean, binwidth = w)] ggplot(data = orientation, aes(x = Bins)) + geom_bar(fill = "grey80", color = "black") + scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, length(seq(0, 360, w))-1, 1), labels = seq(0, 360, w)) + coord_polar(start = -.2) + theme_light() + theme(axis.title = element_blank(), axis.text = element_text(size = 12)) We should also check how burial orientation relates to latitude. Chapter 4 Circular statistics #### DATA #### orientation <- fread("./Data/BurialOrientation.csv", na.strings = "") 4.1 Test: circular statistics with burial sides 4.1.1 Mean and variance #### CIRCULAR MEAN AND VARIANCE #### ## Separate data based on burial side left <- orientation[, .(Num, BurialOrientationMean, BurialOrientationMin, BurialOrientationMax), by = "BurialSide_left"][BurialSide_left == 1] left[, BurialSide := "Left"] right <- orientation[, .(Num, BurialOrientationMean, BurialOrientationMin, BurialOrientationMax), by = "BurialSide_right"][BurialSide_right == 1] right[, BurialSide := "Right"] back <- orientation[, .(Num, BurialOrientationMean, BurialOrientationMin, BurialOrientationMax), by = "BurialSide_back"][BurialSide_back == 1] back[, BurialSide := "Back"] # Bind together in a new table sides <- rbind(left[, -1], right[, -1], back[, -1]) # Example data in degrees sides <- sides[!is.na(BurialOrientationMean)] left_angles <- sides[BurialSide == "Left", BurialOrientationMean] right_angles <- sides[BurialSide == "Right", BurialOrientationMean] back_angles <- sides[BurialSide == "Back", BurialOrientationMean] # Convert to circular objects left_circ <- circular(left_angles, units = "degrees", type = "angles", rotation = "clock") right_circ <- circular(right_angles, units = "degrees", type = "angles", rotation = "clock") back_circ <- circular(back_angles, units = "degrees", type = "angles", rotation = "clock") # Mean direction mean_left <- mean.circular(left_circ) mean_right <- mean.circular(right_circ) mean_back <- mean.circular(back_circ) # Variance direction var_left <- var.circular(left_circ) var_right <- var.circular(right_circ) var_back <- var.circular(back_circ) # Resultant length (measure of concentration) rho_left <- rho.circular(left_circ) rho_right <- rho.circular(right_circ) rho_back <- rho.circular(back_circ) ## Table stats <- data.table(Mean = c(mean_left, mean_right, mean_back), Variance = c(var_left, var_right, var_back), Rho = c(rho_left, rho_right, rho_back), Side = c("Left", "Right", "Back")) stats ## Mean Variance Rho Side ## <circular> <num> <num> <char> ## 1: 116.5037 0.7046924 0.2953076 Left ## 2: 177.3789 0.5876510 0.4123490 Right ## 3: 109.2277 0.7564691 0.2435309 Back 4.1.2 Angular distance Here we create a function to calculate the distance between two angles, taking into account that angles can cross zero. # Function to calculate smallest angular distance angular_distance <- function(a, b) { diff <- abs(a - b) %% 360 return(min(diff, 360 - diff)) } # Example angular_distance(350, 10) ## [1] 20 angular_distance(190, 0) ## [1] 170 # Calculate distances dist_left_right <- angular_distance(as.numeric(mean_left), as.numeric(mean_right)) dist_left_back <- angular_distance(as.numeric(mean_left), as.numeric(mean_back)) dist_right_back <- angular_distance(as.numeric(mean_right), as.numeric(mean_back)) print(dist_left_right) ## [1] 60.87513 print(dist_left_back) ## [1] 7.276052 print(dist_right_back) ## [1] 68.15119 4.1.3 Visualization ## Circular means sides_means <- c(mean_left, mean_right, mean_back) names(sides_means) <- c("Left", "Right", "Back") d <- list() for(a in 1:length(sides_means)){ d[[a]] <- sapply(1:length(sides_means), function(x){ angular_distance(sides_means[a], sides_means[x]) }) } sides_mat <- do.call(cbind, d) colnames(sides_mat) <- rownames(sides_mat) <- names(sides_means) sides_mat[lower.tri(sides_mat)] <- NA sides_dists <- melt(sides_mat) # Plot burial orientations per country sides_means_dt <- data.table(Sides = names(sides_means), Mean = sides_means) sides_means_dt[, Mean := ifelse(Mean < 0, Mean + 360, Mean)] ggplot(data = sides, aes(x = BurialSide, y = BurialOrientationMean, fill = BurialSide)) + geom_violin(width = 1, drop = F) + geom_point(data = sides_means_dt, aes(x = Sides, y = Mean), size = 2, shape = 23, fill = "white") + scale_fill_manual(values = pals::brewer.set2(3)) + ylab("Burial orientation") + theme_light() + theme(legend.position = "none", axis.title.x = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) # Plot pairwise angular distances ggplot(data = sides_dists[!is.na(sides_dists$value),]) + geom_tile(aes(Var1, Var2, fill = value), color = "black") + scale_fill_gradientn("Angular distance", colours = rev(pals::brewer.rdylbu(100)), na.value = "transparent", limits = c(0,180)) + # maximum distance between angles? # guide = guide_colorbar(barwidth = 1, barheight = 15)) + geom_text(aes(Var1, Var2, label = round(value, 1)), size = 10, size.unit = "pt") + scale_x_discrete(position = "top") + ggtitle("Pairwise distance between angles means") + coord_equal(expand = F) + theme_classic() + theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16), axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 0), axis.title = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank(), legend.position = "none", axis.text = element_text(size = 14)) 4.1.4 P-value Now we shuffle the values of angles for each category and compute the differences in circular means and do a histogram where we plot the differences in circular means against the true difference. Do it for each of the three pairs. Make sure that each group has the same amount of observations. n <- min(c(length(left_circ), length(right_circ), length(back_circ))) diffs <- lapply(1:1000, function(x){ l <- sample(left_circ, n) r <- sample(right_circ, n) b <- sample(back_circ, n) mean_l <- mean.circular(l) mean_r <- mean.circular(r) mean_b <- mean.circular(b) dist_lr <- angular_distance(as.numeric(mean_l), as.numeric(mean_r)) dist_lb <- angular_distance(as.numeric(mean_l), as.numeric(mean_b)) dist_br <- angular_distance(as.numeric(mean_b), as.numeric(mean_r)) return(list(dist_lr, dist_lb, dist_br)) }) diffs_lr <- unlist(sapply(diffs, "[", 1)) diffs_lb <- unlist(sapply(diffs, "[", 2)) diffs_br <- unlist(sapply(diffs, "[", 3)) diffs <- list(diffs_lr, diffs_lb, diffs_br) ## Plot histograms hist(diffs_lr, breaks = 100, main = "Difference between left and right orientations", xlab = "Angular distance"); abline(v = dist_left_right, col= "red", lwd = 3) hist(diffs_lb, breaks = 100, main = "Difference between left and back orientations", xlab = "Angular distance"); abline(v = dist_left_back, col= "red", lwd = 3) hist(diffs_br, breaks = 100, main = "Difference between back and right orientations", xlab = "Angular distance"); abline(v = dist_right_back, col= "red", lwd = 3) ## Calculate p-value # P = (X + 1) / (N + 1) obs <- list(dist_left_right, dist_left_back, dist_right_back) pval <- lapply(1:length(diffs), function(x){ X <- sum(abs(diffs[[x]]) >= abs(obs[[x]])) N <- length(diffs[[x]]) return((X + 1) / (N + 1)) }) names(pval) <- c("left_right", "left_back", "back_right") pval ## $left_right ## [1] 0.4815185 ## ## $left_back ## [1] 0.5344655 ## ## $back_right ## [1] 0.4745255 4.1.5 Similarity We can also calculate a similarity index that takes into account the distance between the means of the different categories. # Similarity index similarity_index <- function(d) { return(1 - (d / 180)) } sim_left_right <- similarity_index(dist_left_right) sim_left_back <- similarity_index(dist_left_back) sim_right_back <- similarity_index(dist_right_back) print(sim_left_right) ## [1] 0.6618048 print(sim_left_back) ## [1] 0.9595775 print(sim_right_back) ## [1] 0.6213823 4.1.6 Watson-William test and circular ANOVA ## Watson-Williams test # Combine data all_angles <- c(left_angles, right_angles, back_angles) #right_angles, group <- factor(c(rep("left", length(left_angles)), rep("right", length(right_angles)), rep("back", length(back_angles)))) ## Mardia-Watson-Wheeler test (non-parametric) mww_result1 <- watson.two.test(left_circ, right_circ) # pairwise example mww_result2 <- watson.two.test(left_circ, back_circ) mww_result3 <- watson.two.test(right_circ, back_circ) print(mww_result1) ## ## Watson's Two-Sample Test of Homogeneity ## ## Test Statistic: 2.0137 ## P-value < 0.001 ## print(mww_result2) ## ## Watson's Two-Sample Test of Homogeneity ## ## Test Statistic: 0.3212 ## 0.001 < P-value < 0.01 ## print(mww_result3) ## ## Watson's differences in the orientations of Corded Ware and Bell Beaker cultures. First of all, we look at the summary statistics for the two cultures. We can see that the means (mu) are quite different but the Corded Ware orientations are spread across the whole circle (there is very low concentration). This can be seen both by the rho value (mean resultant length) that is close to 0, and by the variance (var) value that is close to 1 (\(var = 1 - rho\)). The standard deviation runs from 0 to infinity, where higher values indicate a larger dispersion. We can now try and check for differences in mean direction and concentration compared to a uniform distribution. ## Orientations cordedware <- culture[["Corded Ware/Single Grave/Battle Axe/Fatyanovo"]]$BurialOrientationMean cordedware <- circular(cordedware, type = "angles", units = "degrees", rotation = "clock") bellbeaker <- culture[["Bell Beaker complex"]]$BurialOrientationMean bellbeaker <- circular(bellbeaker, type = "angles", units = "degrees", rotation = "clock") ## Summary statistics of the two cultures summary.dat <- data.frame(culture = c("Corded Ware", "Bell Beaker"), mu = c(mean.circular(cordedware), mean.circular(bellbeaker)), rho = c(rho.circular(cordedware), rho.circular(bellbeaker)), var = c(var.circular(cordedware), var.circular(bellbeaker)), sd = c(sd.circular(cordedware), sd.circular(bellbeaker))) summary.dat ## culture mu rho var sd ## 1 Corded Ware -141.30041 0.0224099 0.9775901 2.756176 ## 2 Bell Beaker 77.56884 0.3073971 0.6926029 1.535978 ## Calculate mean direction and concentration from uniform distribution cw_unif <- lapply(1:1000, function(x){ r <- rcircularuniform(n = length(cordedware), control.circular = list( units = "degrees", rotation = "clock")) m <- mean.circular(r) k <- rho.circular(r) return(list(m, k)) }) bb_unif <- lapply(1:1000, function(x){ r <- rcircularuniform(n = length(bellbeaker), control.circular = list( units = "degrees", rotation = "clock")) m <- mean.circular(r) k <- rho.circular(r) return(list(m, k)) }) cw_means <- sapply(cw_unif, "[", 1) cw_rho <- sapply(cw_unif, "[", 2) bb_means <- sapply(bb_unif, "[", 1) bb_rho <- sapply(bb_unif, "[", 2) hist(as.numeric(cw_means), breaks = 100, main = "Corded Ware", xlab = "Mean direction (mu)"); abline(v = mean.circular(cordedware), col = "red") hist(as.numeric(cw_rho), breaks = 100, main = "Corded Ware", xlab = "Concentration (rho)", xlim = c(0,1)); abline(v = rho.circular(cordedware), col = "red") hist(as.numeric(bb_means), breaks = 100, main = "Bell Beaker", xlab = "Mean direction (mu)"); abline(v = mean.circular(bellbeaker), col = "red") hist(as.numeric(bb_rho), breaks = 100, main = "Bell Beaker", xlab = "Concentration (rho)", xlim = c(0,1)); abline(v = rho.circular(bellbeaker), col = "red") # Similarity index (without folding over the horizontal axis) obs <- culture_dists[Var2 == "Corded Ware/Single Grave/Battle Axe/Fatyanovo" & Var1 == "Bell Beaker complex"]$value diff <- similarity_index(obs) diff ## [1] 0.2159403 paste0((1-round(diff,2))*100, "% different") ## [1] "78% different" Now for modelling the differences between the two cultures, we can try using the bpnreg R package. This package performs a Bayesian circular regression model based on the projected normal distribution. The angles must be in radians. This is equivalent to an ANOVA. In this model, the Bell Beaker is the reference culture. Thus, the value of the intercept for the categorical variables represents the mean of the Bell Beaker orientation. Further reading: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2018.02040/full https://bpspsychub.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/bmsp.12108 https://dspace.library.uu.nl/bitstream/handle/1874/361637/1_s2.0_S0022249616300827_main.pdf?sequence=1 # Data for regression circ.dat <- data.frame(Angles = c(as.numeric(cordedware)*pi/180, as.numeric(bellbeaker)*pi/180), Culture = c(rep("Corded Ware", length(cordedware)), rep("Bell Beaker", length(bellbeaker)))) circ.dat$Culture <- as.factor(circ.dat$Culture) fit <- bpnr(Angles ~ 1 + Culture, data = circ.dat, its = 10000, burn = 100, n.lag = 3, seed = 1234) # Means aov.dt <- setDT(data.frame(coef_circ(fit, "categorical", "radians")$Means)) aov.dt[, Culture := as.factor(c("Bell Beaker", "Corded Ware"))] # Plot plot.circular(c(aov.dt$LB[1], aov.dt$UB[1]), pch = 16, rotation = "clock", zero = pi/2) points.circular(c(aov.dt$LB[2], aov.dt$UB[2]), pch = 5, rotation = "clock", zero = pi/2) points.circular(aov.dt$mean[1], pch = 16, col = "red", rotation = "clock", zero = pi/2) points.circular(aov.dt$mean[2], pch = 18, col = "blue", rotation = "clock", zero = pi/2) aov.dt[, .(Culture, deg(.SD)), .SDcols = c("mean", "mode", "sd", "LB", "UB")] ## Culture mean mode sd LB UB ## <fctr> <num> <num> <num> <num> <num> ## 1: Bell Beaker 77.21175 76.68652 9.311352 59.75342 96.56783 ## 2: Corded Ware -142.82673 -163.13410 102.926297 42.10220 14.74897 # Differences diff.dt <- setDT(data.frame(coef_circ(fit, "categorical", units = "degrees")$Differences)) diff.dt[, Difference := "Bell Beaker/Corded Ware"] diff.dt[, .(Difference, mean, mode, sd, LB, UB)] ## Difference mean mode sd LB UB ## <char> <num> <num> <num> <num> <num> ## 1: Bell Beaker/Corded Ware -139.3633 -127.1149 103.2202 24.35254 356.5606 # Calculate angular distance between means angular_distance(aov.dt$mean[1]*180/pi, aov.dt$mean[2]*180/pi) ## [1] 139.9615 In theory the HPDs of the two cultures overlap so the difference in means shouldn’t be significant. When plotting the results, we can see that the two means are quite different and the HPDs overlap only because the spread of the Corded Ware orientations is extremely large. If we look at the differences table, the LB and UP of the HPD for the difference doesn’t cross zero, so the difference between the two cultures is significant. We can also try these other two tests that according to this paper seem to perform well with circular data, without falling too much into Type-1 and Type-2 errors. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-99299-5 ## Watson's U2 test watson.two(cordedware, bellbeaker) ## ## Watson's Two-Sample Test of Homogeneity ## ## Test Statistic: 0.4543 ## P-value < 0.001 ## So when the Watson’s U2 test has a small p-value or a large test statistic, it means that the two groups are NOT homogeneious, so they are significantly different. 4.4.2 Difference between Lažňany and Únětice cultures Now let’s double check that this interpretation is correct by comparing two other very similar cultures, e.g., Lažňany and Únětice. This regression models both the mean direction and the dispersion simultaneously. The model assumes that a circular response variable \(\theta\) has a von Mises distribution with concentration parameter \(\kappa\), and mean direction (\(\mu\)) related to a vector of linear predictor variables according to the relationship: \(\mu + 2*atan(\beta*x)\), where \(\mu\) and \(\beta\) are unknown parameters, \(\beta\) being a vector of regression coefficients, and \(2*atan()\) being the link function. The von Mises distribution is a function of \(\mu\) and \(\kappa\), where \(\mu\) is the mean direction and \(\kappa\) is the concentration parameter. A value \(\kappa = 0\) corresponds to the circular uniform distribution; for \(\kappa > 0\), the density is unimodal and symmetrical about \(\mu\), and increasingly concentrated as \(\kappa\) increases. For \(\kappa \ge 2\) the density at the antipode \(\mu + \pi\) is effectively zero, and the distribution is well approximated by a normal distribution with variance \(1/\kappa\). We can start with an initial value for \(\beta\), to calculate \(\mu\) and \(\kappa\). These estimates can then be used to update the \(\beta\) value, and then to update \(\mu\) and \(\kappa\), analogously to the ML equations for an independent, identically distributed (i.i.d.) von Mises sample. This cycle is repeated until convergence. If \(\beta = 0\), we have a null model where all observations cluster around a common mean direction \(\mu\). However, as the elements of \(\beta\) become infinite, the use of any monotone link function also leads to a null model with mean direction \(\mu ± \pi\). In such cases, the likelihood will have a peak in the vicinity of zero, and attain a similar magnitude as the elements of \(\beta\) tend to \(± \infty\). The optimization process is simplified if the x are centered at their means. So should we scale our ancestry values? (Whether we order the values or scale them, model results don’t seem to change) Further reads: https://www.jstor.org/stable/2532334?seq=2; http://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1742-6596/1988/1/012108 The circular package, has a lm.circular function that can be used for circular and linear data (c-l). We are going to test this function using the ancestry values associated to the grave individuals. 4.6.1 CHG y <- circular(rad(orientation[!is.na(CHG)]$BurialOrientationMean), units = "radians", type = "angles", rotation = "clock") x <- cbind(orientation[!is.na(CHG)]$CHG, rep(1,length(orientation[!is.na(CHG)]$CHG))) colnames(x) <- c("CHG", "Intercept") mu <- as.numeric(mean.circular(y)) reg.chg <- lm.circular(y = y, x = x, type = "c-l", init = c(0,1)) reg.chg ## ## Call: ## lm.circular.cl(y = ..1, x = ..2, init = ..3) ## ## ## Circular-Linear Regression ## ## Coefficients: ## Estimate Std. For continuous explanatory variables we get a set of parameters, bc, SAM and AS, describing its effect on the circle. The coefficient bc represents the slope of the circular regression line at the inflection point. However, this may not be a representative effect for each dataset, as the inflection point can lie in the extremes of the data or even completely outside the range of the predictor x. Therefore, two additional circular coefficients were developed by Cremers et al. (2018), the slope at the mean SAM and the average slope AS. The coefficient SAM represents the slope of the circular regression line at the average of the predictor and the coefficients AS represents the average slope over all values of x. If the HPD intervals for all three circular coefficients (bc, SAM and AS) include 0, we do not find evidence that at the inflection point, at the average predictor value and on average the covariate influences the angular error. https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2018.02040/full#B5 https://bpspsychub.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/bmsp.12108 4.7.1 Full model: space, time, culture, 3 ancestries In the culture models we did above, we saw that culture does seem to be an important predictor of burial orientation. We can now add the three ancestries (CHG, EHG, LVN), the geographic location and time to see if they also are good predictors of orientation. We start with the full model and then we will remove covariates to see which model has the best fit (DIC or WAIC score) to the data. We need to consider that we only have a subset of data with full information about culture and ancestry, so the number of individuals included in the model are less compared to the regressions we did with culture. This will likely change the posterior densities of the coefficients for the cultures, so the circular plot will probably look different than the one above, even for the culture only model. ance.dt <- orientation[, .(Angles = rad(BurialOrientationMean), WHG, CHG, EHG, LVN, Longitude, Latitude, Age, Culture)] ance.dt <- ance.dt[Culture %in% culture_keep] ance.dt <- ance.dt[!is.na(WHG)] ance.dt <- ance.dt[!is.na(Age)] ance.dt <- ance.dt[, .(Angles, scale(.SD), Culture), .SDcols = c("WHG", "EHG", "CHG", "LVN", "Longitude", "Latitude", "Age")] ance.dt$Culture <- factor(ance.dt$Culture, labels = c("Linearbandkeramik", "Lažňany", "Sopot", "Bell Beaker", "Únětice", "Corded Ware", "Baden", "Dnieper-Donets", "Trichterbecher", "Baltic Meso-Neolithic"), levels = unique(ance.dt$Culture)) fit.full <- bpnr(Angles ~ 1 + CHG + EHG + LVN + Latitude + Longitude + Age + Culture, data = ance.dt, its = 10000, burn = 1000, n.lag = 3, seed = 1234) Based on the table for linear coefficients, it seems that none of the ancestries have an effect on the two components (sine, cosine) of the angles. If the HPD interval of the SSDO of a predictor does not include 0, the bivariate regression line does not run through the origin and therefore there is a location effect. Based on this and our HPDs for SSDO, we can conclude that we do not have a location effect. The effect that we see on the two components might therefore be an accuracy effect, an effect on the spread of the angles around the circles and not on the mean direction. SAM is the slope of the regression curve at the mean of the predictor data and the HPDs are outside zero for CHG. When looking at the average slope at each predictor data point (AS), the HPD is outside zero only for CHG.
